source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
When applying topdress fertilizer to growing corn, weeds around the base of each plant should first be cleared away. The fertilizer should then be scattered or placed near the base of the plant (or into a small furrow beside the plant), and covered with soil; it is considered best practice to also hill up/mound soil around the base of the plant at the same time as applying fertilizer.

The source specifically addresses a common farmer question about whether fertilizer can be dissolved in water and sprayed onto the corn crop with a hose, the way farmers commonly do with leafy vegetables such as morning glory (Ipomoea aquatica) or lettuce. It explains that corn differs from these vegetables because it has a much longer growth duration. While corn can absorb some nutrients, water, and air through its leaves, the rate of nutrient loss is higher with foliar (leaf) application compared to soil application. The corn plant's root system plays the primary role in nutrient uptake from the soil, and the leaves cannot fully replace this function. For example, nitrogen applied by spraying onto the leaves makes the crop turn green quickly, but this effect also fades quickly; and if the fertilizer solution is too concentrated, foliar spraying can scorch/burn the corn's leaves. For these reasons, it is better to apply fertilizer into the soil, where the crop can take it up more easily and steadily.
